voltage-converter.quickAnswer: Type the voltage, pick the unit you have and the one you want. Voltage scales by clean powers of ten — 1 kV = 1,000 V and 1 V = 1,000 mV — so conversions are exact.
keyFacts: The volt is the SI unit of electric potential: one joule per coulomb.
Voltage scales by powers of ten: 1,000 mV = 1 V, 1,000 V = 1 kV, 1,000 kV = 1 MV.
Household mains are 230 V (most of the world) or 120 V (North America).
Electronics work in millivolts to volts; power grids run in kilovolts.
High-voltage transmission (hundreds of kV) reduces energy loss over distance.

voltage-converter.formula:
result = value × (from-unit in volts) ÷ (to-unit in volts)
Example: kV = V ÷ 1000
voltage-converter.workedExample:
Convert 230 V to kilovolts.
Step 1: 230 V in volts = 230.
Step 2: 1 kV = 1000 V.
Step 3: 230 ÷ 1000 = 0.23.
Answer: 230 V = 0.23 kV.

faqs.q: How many volts are in a kilovolt?
faqs.a: 1,000 volts. A kilovolt is simply a thousand volts, written 1 kV = 1,000 V.

faqs.q: How do I convert millivolts to volts?
faqs.a: Divide millivolts by 1,000. Example: 3,300 mV ÷ 1,000 = 3.3 V.

faqs.q: What voltage is a car battery?
faqs.a: About 12.6 V when fully charged (a nominal 12 V lead-acid battery). Electric-vehicle packs are hundreds of volts.

faqs.q: Why do power lines use kilovolts?
faqs.a: Higher voltage means lower current for the same power, which cuts resistive heating losses in the wires — so grids transmit at 110–765 kV.

faqs.q: Is 230 V the same as 0.23 kV?
faqs.a: Yes, exactly. 230 ÷ 1,000 = 0.23 kV. Same voltage, different unit.

mistakes: mV vs MV is a billion-fold trap — 5 mV (millivolts) and 5 MV (megavolts) differ by 10⁹. One capital letter changes a sensor reading into a lightning strike.
Converting the number but forgetting AC/DC — 230 V AC and 230 V DC are different beasts. This tool converts magnitude only.
Assuming your mains are 230 V everywhere — North America runs 120 V. Convert the spec, don't assume the socket.
Dividing by 1,000 when you should multiply — 0.5 kV is 500 V, not 0.0005 V. Check the direction before wiring anything.
Treating this as a safety check — the tool does math, not safety. It won't warn you that 400 V can kill.
